stem: The author compares a medieval map to 'an argument' rather than 'a photograph' in order to suggest that such a map
options: was drawn mainly to persuade sailors to adopt particular trade routes
was less valuable than later maps because it relied on written explanations
was designed to communicate a view of the world rather than to record it faithfully
was produced by mapmakers who intentionally falsified distances for profit

verdicts.working: The passage states that medieval maps placed Jerusalem at the centre not out of ignorance, but because they expressed a religious conception of order, making distances secondary to the message conveyed. Comparing the map to 'an argument' rather than 'a photograph' highlights that it was meant to advance a particular worldview/perspective rather than objectively record physical reality.

working: The passage says the Jerusalem-centred map 'expressed a religious conception of order' and that distances and coastlines were secondary to 'the message that the chart was meant to convey'. An argument conveys a viewpoint, whereas a photograph records appearances; hence B. Nothing in the passage mentions persuading sailors, written explanations, or profit-driven falsification.
solution: A photograph records appearances faithfully, whereas an argument puts forward a viewpoint. The passage says the Jerusalem-centred map 'expressed a religious conception of order' and that distances and coastlines were secondary to 'the message that the chart was meant to convey'. So the map was meant to communicate a view of the world, not to record it accurately, which is option (C). The passage says nothing about persuading sailors, relying on written explanations, or falsifying distances for profit, so (A), (B) and (D) are unsupported.
